content.html:
Module 3›Chapter 3.2›Azure DevOps Pipelines: The CI/CD Backbone

What are Azure DevOps Pipelines?

A cloud-hosted CI/CD solution that automates build, test, and deployment processes. It integrates with source control systems like Azure Repos and GitHub.

Why YAML? Pipeline as Code

  • Version Control: Pipeline definitions are stored with your code.
  • Collaboration: Teams can review and contribute to pipeline changes.
  • Consistency: Ensures identical build processes across environments.
  • Recommended Approach: More powerful and flexible than the Classic editor.
Key Takeaway

Azure Pipelines automate CI/CD, with YAML as the preferred method for defining version-controlled, collaborative, and consistent workflows.

# azure-pipelines.yml
trigger:
  - main

pool:
  vmImage: 'ubuntu-latest'

stages:
  - stage: Build
    jobs:
      - job: BuildJob
        steps:
          - script: echo "Hello, CI!"
# YAML structure for a basic CI pipeline
# Defines triggers, agent pool, stages, jobs, and steps.

screens.title: Triggers and Agent Pools
screens.narratorSegment: Let's start by exploring two fundamental components of an Azure Pipeline: trigger and pool. The trigger section is where you define the events that will automatically start your pipeline. The most common triggers are push events to specific branches, such as main or develop, or pull underscore request events. You can also refine these triggers with path filters, ensuring the pipeline only runs if changes occur in particular directories. For instance, specifying trigger. - main means your pipeline will execute every time code is pushed to the main branch. This ensures continuous validation of your main codebase. Next, the pool section specifies the agent pool where your pipeline jobs will run. An agent is essentially a piece of software that executes the tasks defined in your pipeline. Azure DevOps provides Microsoft-hosted agents, which are pre-configured virtual machines running Windows, Linux, or Mac O S. These are managed entirely by Azure and are incredibly convenient for public projects or when you don't have unique environment requirements. For example, pool. vm Image. 'ubuntu-latest' will instruct your pipeline to use the latest Ubuntu-based Microsoft-hosted agent. This simplicity makes them a popular choice for many CI scenarios.

keyIdea.text: Triggers define pipeline start events, while agent pools specify the execution environment, often using convenient Microsoft-hosted agents.

content.html:
Module 3›Chapter 3.2›Triggers and Agent Pools

1. `trigger` Section

  • Purpose: Defines events that start your pipeline.
  • Common Triggers: push to branches (e.g., main, develop), pull_request events.
  • Path Filters: Restrict triggers to specific directories.
  • Example: trigger: - main runs on every push to the main branch.

2. `pool` Section (Microsoft-hosted Agents)

  • Purpose: Specifies the agent pool where jobs run.
  • Agents: Software that executes pipeline jobs.
  • Microsoft-hosted: Pre-configured VMs (Windows, Linux, macOS) managed by Azure.
  • Benefits: Zero setup, always up-to-date, convenient for public projects.
  • Example: pool: vmImage: 'ubuntu-latest' uses the latest Ubuntu agent.
Key Takeaway

Triggers automate pipeline starts, while agent pools provide the execution environment, with Microsoft-hosted agents offering ease of use for many scenarios.

# azure-pipelines.yml
trigger:
  - main
  # - pull_request
  # branches:
  # - develop
  # paths:
  # - 'src/*'

pool:
  vmImage: 'ubuntu-latest'
  # Or 'windows-latest', 'macos-latest'
# 'trigger' defines when the pipeline runs.
# 'pool' specifies the agent environment.

screens.title: Self-Hosted Agents: Custom Environments
screens.narratorSegment: While Microsoft-hosted agents are incredibly convenient, there are scenarios where you need more control over your build environment. This is where self-hosted agents come into play. A self-hosted agent is a machine, either physical or virtual, that you set up and manage yourself. You install the agent software on your own infrastructure, giving you complete control over its operating system, installed software, and hardware specifications. This flexibility is invaluable when your project requires specific software versions that aren't available on Microsoft-hosted agents, or perhaps custom hardware like GPUs for machine learning workloads. A significant advantage of self-hosted agents is their ability to access resources within your private network. This is crucial for building legacy applications that rely on internal databases or file shares, or for deploying to on-premises servers that are not publicly accessible. However, this control comes with responsibility: you are accountable for the setup, maintenance, scaling, security, and updates of these agents. It's a trade-off between convenience and customization, and choosing the right agent type depends heavily on your project's unique requirements and constraints. For example, if you need to build an old C++ application with a specific compiler version from 2005, a self-hosted agent is likely your only viable option.

content.html:
Module 3›Chapter 3.2›Self-Hosted Agents: Custom Environments

What are Self-Hosted Agents?

  • Machines (physical or virtual) that you set up and manage.
  • You install the Azure DevOps agent software.
  • Provides full control over the environment.

Key Advantages

  • Custom Software: Install specific versions or proprietary tools.
  • Private Network Access: Reach internal resources (databases, file shares).
  • Dedicated Resources: Utilize specific hardware (e.g., GPUs) or ensure consistent performance.
  • Security: Maintain strict control over the build environment.
Key Takeaway

Self-hosted agents offer unparalleled control and private network access, making them ideal for specialized, legacy, or highly secure build environments.

# azure-pipelines.yml
pool:
  name: 'MyPrivateAgentPool'
  demands:
    - MSBuild
    - VisualStudio

# Example: Using a self-hosted agent pool named 'MyPrivateAgentPool'
# with specific capabilities (demands) like MSBuild and VisualStudio.
# Self-hosted agents provide custom environments.
# Use 'name' to specify your custom agent pool.

screens.title: Stages and Jobs: Organizing Your Workflow
screens.narratorSegment: As your CI/CD pipelines grow in complexity, organizing them effectively becomes crucial. Azure Pipelines allow you to structure your workflow using stages and jobs. Stages represent major phases of your pipeline, such as Build, Test, or Deploy. Think of them as high-level containers that group related work. By default, stages run sequentially, meaning the 'Build' stage must complete before the 'Test' stage begins. However, you can configure dependencies to control their execution order, allowing for more intricate workflows. While a simple CI pipeline might only have one stage, multi-stage pipelines are essential for complex CI/CD scenarios that involve distinct phases like building, testing, and then deploying to different environments. Within each stage, you define one or more jobs. A job is a collection of steps that run together on a single agent. Jobs are powerful because they can run in parallel by default, which significantly speeds up your pipelines. For example, you could have one job running unit tests and another running linting checks simultaneously. Each job can also specify its own pool, meaning different jobs within the same stage can utilize different types of agents if required. This granular control over execution environments and parallelism makes jobs a key component for optimizing pipeline performance and resource utilization.

content.html:
Module 3›Chapter 3.2›Stages and Jobs: Organizing Your Workflow

3. `stages` Section

  • Purpose: Organize pipelines into major phases (e.g., Build, Test, Deploy).
  • Execution: Run sequentially by default; dependencies can be configured.
  • Use Case: Crucial for complex CI/CD workflows with distinct phases.
  • Example: A 'Build' stage followed by a 'Test' stage.

4. `jobs` Section

  • Purpose: A collection of steps that run together on a single agent.
  • Execution: Can run in parallel by default, speeding up pipelines.
  • Agent Specificity: Each job can specify its own pool.
  • Example: One job for unit tests, another for linting, running concurrently.
Key Takeaway

Stages define major pipeline phases, while jobs group steps for parallel execution on agents, enabling modular and efficient CI/CD workflows.

# azure-pipelines.yml
stages:
  - stage: Build
    displayName: 'Build Application'
    jobs:
      - job: CompileJob
        displayName: 'Compile Code'
        steps:
          - script: echo "Compiling..."
      - job: LintJob
        displayName: 'Run Linting'
        steps:
          - script: echo "Linting..."

- stage: Test
  displayName: 'Run Tests'
  dependsOn: Build
  jobs:
    - job: UnitTests
      steps:
        - script: echo "Running unit tests..."
# Stages define major phases (Build, Test).
# Jobs within stages can run in parallel.

screens.title: Steps: The Core of Execution
screens.narratorSegment: At the most granular level of an Azure Pipeline, we find steps. These are the individual tasks or scripts that a job executes, forming the smallest building blocks of your pipeline. Steps are where the actual work happens, whether it's compiling code, running tests, or deploying an application. You can define steps in two primary ways. First, as scripts, which are inline shell commands or references to script files. For example, script. echo Hello would simply print 'Hello' to the console during the pipeline run. This is useful for simple commands or custom logic. Second, and more commonly, steps can be defined as tasks. Tasks are pre-built operations provided by Azure DevOps or available through the Marketplace. These tasks abstract away complex logic, making it easier to perform common operations. Examples include Dot Net Core CLI@2 for. NET applications, Npm@1 for Node. js projects, or Azure Rm Web App Deployment@4 for deploying to Azure App Services. Notice the version number, like @2 in Dot Net Core CLI@2; this ensures compatibility and allows you to use specific versions of a task. Using tasks is generally recommended as they are maintained, tested, and often provide more robust error handling and logging than custom scripts. For instance, instead of writing a complex script to restore NuGet packages, you can simply use the Dot Net Core CLI@2 task with the 'restore' command, which is much more efficient and reliable.

content.html:
Module 3›Chapter 3.2›Steps: The Core of Execution

5. `steps` Section

  • Purpose: Individual tasks or scripts executed by a job.
  • Smallest Building Blocks: Where the actual work of the pipeline occurs.

Types of Steps

  • Scripts: Inline shell commands (script: echo Hello) or references to script files.
  • Tasks: Pre-built, versioned operations from Azure DevOps or Marketplace.
    • Example: DotNetCoreCLI@2 for .NET, Npm@1 for Node.js.
    • Recommended for robustness and ease of use.
Key Takeaway

Steps are the fundamental actions in a pipeline, executed as custom scripts or robust, pre-built tasks for efficient and reliable automation.

# azure-pipelines.yml
steps:
  - checkout: self
    displayName: 'Checkout Code'

  - task: DotNetCoreCLI@2
    displayName: 'Restore NuGet Packages'
    inputs:
      command: 'restore'
      projects: '**/*.csproj'

  - script: echo "Custom build step"
    displayName: 'Run Custom Script'
# 'checkout' is a special step to get source code.
# 'task' uses pre-built operations.
# 'script' runs inline commands.

screens.title: Building a .NET Core CI Pipeline (Part 1)
screens.narratorSegment: Now, let's put these concepts into practice by walking through a minimal YAML pipeline example for a. NET Core application. This example will demonstrate how the core components we've discussed come together to form a functional CI workflow. Our pipeline begins with the trigger section, configured to run on every push to the main branch. This ensures that any new code merged into main is immediately validated. Next, we specify the pool for our agent. For this. NET Core application, we'll use a Microsoft-hosted agent with vm Image. 'windows-latest'. This provides a convenient, pre-configured Windows environment with all the necessary. NET tools installed, requiring zero setup from our side. The pipeline then defines a single stage named Build, with a display Name of 'Build Application'. Within this stage, we have one job called Build Job, which is responsible for compiling and testing our code. The first step in this job is checkout. self, which simply checks out the source code from our repository onto the agent. This is a crucial initial step for any pipeline. Following this, we use the Dot Net Core CLI@2 task to 'Restore NuGet Packages'. This task efficiently downloads all project dependencies, ensuring our build environment is complete before compilation. This structured approach ensures clarity and maintainability.

keyIdea.title: Initial Pipeline Setup
keyIdea.text: A .NET Core CI pipeline starts with a `main` branch trigger, uses a `windows-latest` agent, and includes steps to checkout code and restore NuGet packages.

content.html:
Module 3›Chapter 3.2›Building a .NET Core CI Pipeline (Part 1)

Pipeline Configuration

  • Trigger: - main (runs on pushes to the main branch).
  • Agent Pool: vmImage: 'windows-latest' (Microsoft-hosted Windows agent).
  • Stage: Build (main phase for application build).
  • Job: BuildJob (compiles and tests the application).

Initial Steps

  • Checkout Code: checkout: self retrieves source from the repository.
  • Restore NuGet Packages: DotNetCoreCLI@2 with command: 'restore' downloads all project dependencies.
Key Takeaway

A robust CI pipeline starts with clear triggers and agent selection, followed by essential steps like code checkout and dependency restoration.

# azure-pipelines.yml
trigger:
- main

pool:
  vmImage: 'windows-latest'

stages:
- stage: Build
  displayName: Build Application
  jobs:
  - job: BuildJob
    displayName: Compile and Test
    steps:

screens.narratorSegment: Continuing our. NET Core CI pipeline example, after restoring NuGet packages, the next logical step is to build the project. We again use the Dot Net Core CLI@2 task, this time with the command. 'build' and arguments. '--configuration Release' to compile our application in the Release configuration. This ensures that our code is compiled and ready for testing and potential deployment. Following a successful build, it's critical to run unit tests to validate the code's functionality. We use another Dot Net Core CLI@2 task, specifying command. 'test' and targeting projects ending with asterisk Tests. csproj. We also include arguments. '--configuration Release --logger trx' to run tests in Release mode and output the results in TRX format, which is a standard format for test results in the Microsoft ecosystem. Once tests are executed, we need to make their outcomes visible within Azure DevOps. This is achieved using the Publish Test Results@2 task. We configure it to look for asterisk asterisk slash asterisk. trx files, merge the results, and crucially, fail Task On Failed Tests. true. This setting ensures that if any unit tests fail, the entire pipeline run will be marked as a failure, immediately alerting developers to issues. This immediate feedback loop is a cornerstone of effective Continuous Integration, preventing broken code from progressing further in the development cycle. It's a powerful mechanism for maintaining code quality.

Module 3›Chapter 3.2›Building a .NET Core CI Pipeline (Part 2)

Build and Test Steps

  • Build Project: DotNetCoreCLI@2 with command: 'build' and --configuration Release.
  • Run Unit Tests: Another DotNetCoreCLI@2 task with command: 'test', targeting *Tests.csproj and outputting --logger trx.

Publish Test Results

  • Task: PublishTestResults@2.
  • Configuration: Looks for **/*.trx files, merges results.
  • Critical Setting: failTaskOnFailedTests: true ensures pipeline failure on test failures, providing immediate feedback.
Key Takeaway

After building, running unit tests and publishing their results with a fail-on-failure policy is crucial for maintaining code quality and rapid feedback.

# ... (previous steps)

    - task: DotNetCoreCLI@2
      displayName: Build Project
      inputs:
        command: 'build'
        projects: '**/*.csproj'
        arguments: '--configuration Release'

    - task: DotNetCoreCLI@2
      displayName: Run Unit Tests
      inputs:
        command: 'test'
        projects: '**/*Tests.csproj'
        arguments: '--configuration Release --logger trx'

    - task: PublishTestResults@2
      displayName: Publish Test Results
      inputs:
        testResultsFormat: 'VSTest'
        testResultsFiles: '**/*.trx'
        mergeTestResults: true
        failTaskOnFailedTests: true
# Build the project in Release configuration.
# Run unit tests and generate TRX reports.
# Publish test results and fail if tests fail.

screens.narratorSegment: The final crucial step in our. NET Core CI pipeline is to publish the build artifacts. After successfully building and testing our application, we need to save the compiled output so it can be consumed by subsequent stages, such as a deployment pipeline, or by other pipelines entirely. This is where the Publish Build Artifacts@1 task comes in. This task is responsible for taking the output of your build and making it available in Azure DevOps' artifact store. We configure it with path To Publish. '$ open parenthesis Build. Artifact Staging Directory close parenthesis '. The $ open parenthesis Build. Artifact Staging Directory close parenthesis is a predefined variable in Azure DevOps that points to a local path on the agent where artifacts should be copied before being published. This ensures that all necessary files are collected in a single, organized location. We then give our artifact a artifact Name. 'drop', which is a common convention for naming the primary build output. Finally, publish Location. 'Container' specifies that the artifact should be published to the Azure DevOps artifact store, making it easily accessible within your project. Publishing artifacts is a vital practice for any CI pipeline, as it creates a clear, versioned output that can be reliably used for deployment, archiving, or sharing with other teams. Without this step, your successful build would essentially be lost, unable to be deployed or reused. It's the bridge between your CI and CD processes.

screens.title: Microsoft-Hosted vs. Self-Hosted Agents: A Comparison
screens.narratorSegment: Deciding between Microsoft-hosted and self-hosted agents is a critical choice that impacts your pipeline's flexibility, cost, and maintenance. Let's compare them in detail. Microsoft-hosted agents offer significant advantages: zero setup and maintenance, as Azure manages everything for you. They are always up-to-date with the latest tools and provide a wide range of pre-installed software, scaling automatically to meet demand. This makes them ideal for most common CI scenarios, especially open-source projects or cloud-native applications where specific environment customization isn't a primary concern. However, they do have limitations, such as limited customization options, potential lack of specific legacy software, and no direct access to private network resources. Performance can also vary as it's a shared environment. On the other hand, self-hosted agents provide full control over the environment, allowing for custom software, specific hardware, and crucial access to private networks. This is invaluable for building legacy applications, deploying to on-premises servers, or meeting strict network security requirements. The trade-off is that you are responsible for their setup, maintenance, scaling, security, and updates. A common misconception is that self-hosted agents are always better due to control; however, for many projects, the ease and cost-effectiveness of Microsoft-hosted agents make them the superior choice. Always evaluate your project's specific needs before making a decision.

screens.title: Avoiding Common Pipeline Mistakes
screens.narratorSegment: As you begin to build and manage Azure Pipelines, it's important to be aware of common pitfalls that can lead to frustration and pipeline failures. One of the most frequent mistakes is incorrect YAML indentation. YAML is whitespace-sensitive, meaning even a single extra space can break your pipeline definition. Always use a YAML linter or a good IDE with YAML support to validate your syntax. Another common issue is specifying non-existent tasks or inputs. Double-check task names and their required parameters against the official documentation or the Marketplace. A task like Dot Net Core CLI@2 expects specific inputs, and a typo can cause the pipeline to fail. Furthermore, selecting an agent pool that lacks the necessary tools or operating system for your build is a frequent error. For example, trying to build a. NET Framework application on an Ubuntu agent will obviously fail. Always ensure your agent pool matches your project's requirements. For self-hosted agents, remember to verify that the agent software is running, and that the agent has the necessary permissions and network access to perform its tasks. Finally, safety considerations are paramount. Ensure that agent service accounts operate with the principle of least privilege, having only the permissions absolutely required. Self-hosted agents, being part of your infrastructure, must also be kept secure and regularly updated to prevent vulnerabilities. By being mindful of these common mistakes and security practices, you can build more reliable and secure CI/CD pipelines.

content.html:
Module 3›Chapter 3.2›Avoiding Common Pipeline Mistakes

Common Mistakes

  • Incorrect YAML Indentation: YAML is whitespace-sensitive. Use linters!
  • Non-existent Tasks/Inputs: Verify task names and parameters against documentation.
  • Mismatched Agent Pool: Ensure the agent's OS and tools match project requirements.
  • Self-hosted Agent Issues: Verify agent software is running, and it has correct permissions/network access.

Safety Considerations

  • Least Privilege: Agent service accounts should have only necessary permissions.
  • Security & Updates: Keep self-hosted agents secure and regularly updated.
Key Takeaway

Validate YAML, match agents to project needs, and prioritize security with least privilege and regular updates to build robust and reliable pipelines.

Troubleshooting Checklist

  • Is your YAML syntax valid? (Check indentation!)
  • Are all tasks and their inputs correctly spelled and configured?
  • Does your agent pool have the required OS and software?
  • For self-hosted agents, is the service running and does it have network access?
  • Are agent permissions restricted to only what's necessary?

fullNarratorScript:
Welcome to this chapter on setting up Azure DevOps Pipelines for Continuous Integration. In today's fast-paced development environment, automating your build and test processes is not just a luxury, but a necessity. Azure DevOps Pipelines provide a powerful, cloud-hosted solution that integrates seamlessly with your source control, whether it's Azure Repos or GitHub. By the end of this session, you'll understand the core components of an Azure Pipeline, how to define them using YAML, and how to choose the right execution environment for your projects. We'll explore how these pipelines act as the backbone of modern CI/CD, ensuring that every code change is automatically validated, leading to more stable and reliable software releases. This foundational knowledge is crucial for any DevOps engineer looking to streamline development workflows and deliver value faster. Let's dive in and unlock the power of automated CI with Azure DevOps.

In this chapter, we'll focus on two key objectives to build your expertise in Azure DevOps Pipelines. First, you will gain a deep understanding of the fundamental components that make up an Azure DevOps Pipeline. This includes triggers, which initiate your pipeline, agents that execute your jobs, and the organizational structure of stages, jobs, and individual steps. Knowing these building blocks is crucial for designing any effective CI workflow, allowing you to visualize how your code moves through the automated process. Second, you will learn to create a basic YAML-based Azure Pipeline. This practical skill involves writing the azure-pipelines. yml file from scratch to build a sample application. This hands-on experience will solidify your understanding of 'pipeline as code' and enable you to start automating your own projects immediately. These objectives are foundational for anyone looking to implement robust and maintainable CI/CD practices.

Continuing our journey, the next objective is to configure agent pools and specify execution environments for your pipeline jobs. This involves understanding how to direct your build and test tasks to the correct type of machine, whether it's a Windows, Linux, or Mac O S environment. Proper agent configuration ensures your pipeline has all the necessary tools and resources to execute successfully, preventing common build failures due to missing dependencies. Finally, you will learn to differentiate between Microsoft-hosted and self-hosted agents, and identify the appropriate use cases for each. This distinction is vital for making informed decisions about cost, control, and access to private network resources. For example, a public open-source project might benefit from Microsoft-hosted agents, while a legacy application requiring specific compilers might need a self-hosted agent. Mastering these choices will empower you to optimize your CI infrastructure for various project requirements.

Azure DevOps Pipelines offer a robust, cloud-hosted solution for Continuous Integration and Continuous Delivery, seamlessly integrating with various source control systems like Azure Repos and GitHub. At its heart, an Azure Pipeline is a sequence of automated steps designed to execute upon specific events, such as a code commit or a pull request. This automation is critical for maintaining code quality and accelerating delivery cycles. The modern and recommended way to define these pipelines is through a YAML file, typically named azure-pipelines. yml, which is stored directly within your source code repository. This 'pipeline as code' approach brings significant advantages, including version control for your build definitions, enhanced collaboration among team members, and ensuring consistency across different environments. While a graphical user interface, known as the Classic editor, is available, YAML pipelines are generally preferred for their power and flexibility, especially in complex CI/CD scenarios. Understanding this fundamental shift to YAML is key to mastering Azure Pipelines. Azure DevOps Pipelines: The CI/CD Backbone means azure pipelines automate ci/cd using yaml files stored in source control, offering versioning, collaboration, and consistency.. In practical terms, automating your development workflow with cloud-hosted solutions.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Let's start by exploring two fundamental components of an Azure Pipeline: trigger and pool. The trigger section is where you define the events that will automatically start your pipeline. The most common triggers are push events to specific branches, such as main or develop, or pull underscore request events. You can also refine these triggers with path filters, ensuring the pipeline only runs if changes occur in particular directories. For instance, specifying trigger. - main means your pipeline will execute every time code is pushed to the main branch. This ensures continuous validation of your main codebase. Next, the pool section specifies the agent pool where your pipeline jobs will run. An agent is essentially a piece of software that executes the tasks defined in your pipeline. Azure DevOps provides Microsoft-hosted agents, which are pre-configured virtual machines running Windows, Linux, or Mac O S. These are managed entirely by Azure and are incredibly convenient for public projects or when you don't have unique environment requirements. For example, pool. vm Image. 'ubuntu-latest' will instruct your pipeline to use the latest Ubuntu-based Microsoft-hosted agent. This simplicity makes them a popular choice for many CI scenarios.

While Microsoft-hosted agents are incredibly convenient, there are scenarios where you need more control over your build environment. This is where self-hosted agents come into play. A self-hosted agent is a machine, either physical or virtual, that you set up and manage yourself. You install the agent software on your own infrastructure, giving you complete control over its operating system, installed software, and hardware specifications. This flexibility is invaluable when your project requires specific software versions that aren't available on Microsoft-hosted agents, or perhaps custom hardware like GPUs for machine learning workloads. A significant advantage of self-hosted agents is their ability to access resources within your private network. This is crucial for building legacy applications that rely on internal databases or file shares, or for deploying to on-premises servers that are not publicly accessible. However, this control comes with responsibility: you are accountable for the setup, maintenance, scaling, security, and updates of these agents. It's a trade-off between convenience and customization, and choosing the right agent type depends heavily on your project's unique requirements and constraints. For example, if you need to build an old C++ application with a specific compiler version from 2005, a self-hosted agent is likely your only viable option.

As your CI/CD pipelines grow in complexity, organizing them effectively becomes crucial. Azure Pipelines allow you to structure your workflow using stages and jobs. Stages represent major phases of your pipeline, such as Build, Test, or Deploy. Think of them as high-level containers that group related work. By default, stages run sequentially, meaning the 'Build' stage must complete before the 'Test' stage begins. However, you can configure dependencies to control their execution order, allowing for more intricate workflows. While a simple CI pipeline might only have one stage, multi-stage pipelines are essential for complex CI/CD scenarios that involve distinct phases like building, testing, and then deploying to different environments. Within each stage, you define one or more jobs. A job is a collection of steps that run together on a single agent. Jobs are powerful because they can run in parallel by default, which significantly speeds up your pipelines. For example, you could have one job running unit tests and another running linting checks simultaneously. Each job can also specify its own pool, meaning different jobs within the same stage can utilize different types of agents if required. This granular control over execution environments and parallelism makes jobs a key component for optimizing pipeline performance and resource utilization.

At the most granular level of an Azure Pipeline, we find steps. These are the individual tasks or scripts that a job executes, forming the smallest building blocks of your pipeline. Steps are where the actual work happens, whether it's compiling code, running tests, or deploying an application. You can define steps in two primary ways. First, as scripts, which are inline shell commands or references to script files. For example, script. echo Hello would simply print 'Hello' to the console during the pipeline run. This is useful for simple commands or custom logic. Second, and more commonly, steps can be defined as tasks. Tasks are pre-built operations provided by Azure DevOps or available through the Marketplace. These tasks abstract away complex logic, making it easier to perform common operations. Examples include Dot Net Core CLI@2 for. NET applications, Npm@1 for Node. js projects, or Azure Rm Web App Deployment@4 for deploying to Azure App Services. Notice the version number, like @2 in Dot Net Core CLI@2; this ensures compatibility and allows you to use specific versions of a task. Using tasks is generally recommended as they are maintained, tested, and often provide more robust error handling and logging than custom scripts. For instance, instead of writing a complex script to restore NuGet packages, you can simply use the Dot Net Core CLI@2 task with the 'restore' command, which is much more efficient and reliable.

Now, let's put these concepts into practice by walking through a minimal YAML pipeline example for a. NET Core application. This example will demonstrate how the core components we've discussed come together to form a functional CI workflow. Our pipeline begins with the trigger section, configured to run on every push to the main branch. This ensures that any new code merged into main is immediately validated. Next, we specify the pool for our agent. For this. NET Core application, we'll use a Microsoft-hosted agent with vm Image. 'windows-latest'. This provides a convenient, pre-configured Windows environment with all the necessary. NET tools installed, requiring zero setup from our side. The pipeline then defines a single stage named Build, with a display Name of 'Build Application'. Within this stage, we have one job called Build Job, which is responsible for compiling and testing our code. The first step in this job is checkout. self, which simply checks out the source code from our repository onto the agent. This is a crucial initial step for any pipeline. Following this, we use the Dot Net Core CLI@2 task to 'Restore NuGet Packages'. This task efficiently downloads all project dependencies, ensuring our build environment is complete before compilation. This structured approach ensures clarity and maintainability.

Continuing our. NET Core CI pipeline example, after restoring NuGet packages, the next logical step is to build the project. We again use the Dot Net Core CLI@2 task, this time with the command. 'build' and arguments. '--configuration Release' to compile our application in the Release configuration. This ensures that our code is compiled and ready for testing and potential deployment. Following a successful build, it's critical to run unit tests to validate the code's functionality. We use another Dot Net Core CLI@2 task, specifying command. 'test' and targeting projects ending with asterisk Tests. csproj. We also include arguments. '--configuration Release --logger trx' to run tests in Release mode and output the results in TRX format, which is a standard format for test results in the Microsoft ecosystem. Once tests are executed, we need to make their outcomes visible within Azure DevOps. This is achieved using the Publish Test Results@2 task. We configure it to look for asterisk asterisk slash asterisk. trx files, merge the results, and crucially, fail Task On Failed Tests. true. This setting ensures that if any unit tests fail, the entire pipeline run will be marked as a failure, immediately alerting developers to issues. This immediate feedback loop is a cornerstone of effective Continuous Integration, preventing broken code from progressing further in the development cycle. It's a powerful mechanism for maintaining code quality.

The final crucial step in our. NET Core CI pipeline is to publish the build artifacts. After successfully building and testing our application, we need to save the compiled output so it can be consumed by subsequent stages, such as a deployment pipeline, or by other pipelines entirely. This is where the Publish Build Artifacts@1 task comes in. This task is responsible for taking the output of your build and making it available in Azure DevOps' artifact store. We configure it with path To Publish. '$ open parenthesis Build. Artifact Staging Directory close parenthesis '. The $ open parenthesis Build. Artifact Staging Directory close parenthesis is a predefined variable in Azure DevOps that points to a local path on the agent where artifacts should be copied before being published. This ensures that all necessary files are collected in a single, organized location. We then give our artifact a artifact Name. 'drop', which is a common convention for naming the primary build output. Finally, publish Location. 'Container' specifies that the artifact should be published to the Azure DevOps artifact store, making it easily accessible within your project. Publishing artifacts is a vital practice for any CI pipeline, as it creates a clear, versioned output that can be reliably used for deployment, archiving, or sharing with other teams. Without this step, your successful build would essentially be lost, unable to be deployed or reused. It's the bridge between your CI and CD processes.

Deciding between Microsoft-hosted and self-hosted agents is a critical choice that impacts your pipeline's flexibility, cost, and maintenance. Let's compare them in detail. Microsoft-hosted agents offer significant advantages: zero setup and maintenance, as Azure manages everything for you. They are always up-to-date with the latest tools and provide a wide range of pre-installed software, scaling automatically to meet demand. This makes them ideal for most common CI scenarios, especially open-source projects or cloud-native applications where specific environment customization isn't a primary concern. However, they do have limitations, such as limited customization options, potential lack of specific legacy software, and no direct access to private network resources. Performance can also vary as it's a shared environment. On the other hand, self-hosted agents provide full control over the environment, allowing for custom software, specific hardware, and crucial access to private networks. This is invaluable for building legacy applications, deploying to on-premises servers, or meeting strict network security requirements. The trade-off is that you are responsible for their setup, maintenance, scaling, security, and updates. A common misconception is that self-hosted agents are always better due to control; however, for many projects, the ease and cost-effectiveness of Microsoft-hosted agents make them the superior choice. Always evaluate your project's specific needs before making a decision.

As you begin to build and manage Azure Pipelines, it's important to be aware of common pitfalls that can lead to frustration and pipeline failures. One of the most frequent mistakes is incorrect YAML indentation. YAML is whitespace-sensitive, meaning even a single extra space can break your pipeline definition. Always use a YAML linter or a good IDE with YAML support to validate your syntax. Another common issue is specifying non-existent tasks or inputs. Double-check task names and their required parameters against the official documentation or the Marketplace. A task like Dot Net Core CLI@2 expects specific inputs, and a typo can cause the pipeline to fail. Furthermore, selecting an agent pool that lacks the necessary tools or operating system for your build is a frequent error. For example, trying to build a. NET Framework application on an Ubuntu agent will obviously fail. Always ensure your agent pool matches your project's requirements. For self-hosted agents, remember to verify that the agent software is running, and that the agent has the necessary permissions and network access to perform its tasks. Finally, safety considerations are paramount. Ensure that agent service accounts operate with the principle of least privilege, having only the permissions absolutely required. Self-hosted agents, being part of your infrastructure, must also be kept secure and regularly updated to prevent vulnerabilities. By being mindful of these common mistakes and security practices, you can build more reliable and secure CI/CD pipelines.

Let's recap some of the most important concepts from this chapter. First, Azure DevOps Pipelines are a cloud service providing robust CI/CD capabilities, automating the build, test, and deployment of your code. They are the central nervous system for modern software delivery. Second, the YAML Pipeline represents a 'pipeline as code' approach, where your pipeline definition is stored directly in your source code repository. This brings immense benefits like version control, collaboration, and consistency. Finally, an Agent Pool is a collection of agents available to run jobs in a pipeline. These agents are the workhorses that execute your defined steps. Understanding these core ideas is fundamental to effectively leveraging Azure DevOps for your continuous integration needs. They form the bedrock upon which all your automated workflows will be built, ensuring that your development process is efficient, repeatable, and reliable. Keep these definitions in mind as you design your own pipelines.

Continuing our review of key concepts, it's important to distinguish between agent types. Microsoft-hosted Agents are virtual machines managed by Azure DevOps, pre-configured with common tools, offering zero maintenance. They are excellent for general-purpose builds. In contrast, Self-hosted Agents are machines you set up and manage yourself, providing full control over the environment. These are ideal for specialized software or private network access. Lastly, a Stage is a logical division in a pipeline that groups related jobs, typically representing a major phase like Build, Test, or Deploy. Stages help organize complex pipelines into manageable, sequential steps. Understanding these distinctions and organizational structures will enable you to design and implement highly effective and tailored CI/CD solutions. Remember, the choice of agent and the structure of your pipeline directly impact its efficiency, security, and maintainability. By mastering these concepts, you're well on your way to becoming a proficient DevOps engineer.
